title: Burgundy
description: A narrow strip of limestone slopes where single vineyards, called climats, have been mapped for a thousand years.
L: Explain the role of the monks

Burgundy, Bourgogne, runs about 230 km from Chablis in the north to the Mâconnais in the south, in eastern France. Its heart is the Côte d'Or, a narrow, east-facing escarpment of limestone and marl. It has about 30,000 hectares of vines, smaller than Bordeaux, but over 1,200 named vineyard sites.

Burgundy's climate is continental: cold winters, warm summers and risk at every stage. Spring frost can destroy buds, as in 2016 and 2021. Hail can strip vineyards in minutes. Rain at harvest brings rot. Slopes and east-facing exposure help: they catch morning sun and let cold air drain away.
Why do Burgundy's best vineyards face east?
They catch morning sun and drain cold air
East-facing slopes warm early and avoid frost pockets.

From the 10th century, Benedictine monks of Cluny and Cistercians of Cîteaux studied Burgundy's slopes. They noticed that wines from small plots tasted consistently different and enclosed them with walls, called clos, like Clos de Vougeot. These named plots, the climats, were recognised by UNESCO as World Heritage in 2015.
Burgundy's climats were recognised by UNESCO in 2015.
Yes, as a World Heritage Site.
Burgundy runs from Chablis to the Mâconnais
Its continental climate brings frost, hail and rot
Monks mapped the climats, now UNESCO-listed
Two great grapes and two more

Burgundy's two great grapes are Pinot Noir, for reds, and Chardonnay, for whites. Unlike Bordeaux, Burgundy rarely blends: each wine is usually a single grape from a single place. The idea is that the climat, not the blend, gives the wine its character.

Aligoté, a sibling of Chardonnay, makes crisp, lemony whites; Bouzeron, in the Côte Chalonnaise, is its own appellation. Aligoté is the traditional base of the Kir, with blackcurrant liqueur. Gamay, banned from the Côte d'Or in 1395, grows mainly in Beaujolais, though it's allowed in some Burgundy blends like Coteaux Bourguignons.
Match each grape to its role.
Burgundy is a land of single grapes.
Order a Kir in Burgundy and you'll get Aligoté with crème de cassis, named after Félix Kir, a mayor of Dijon.
Why does Burgundy rarely blend grapes?
It aims to show the character of each climat
A single grape lets the site speak.
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are Burgundy's great grapes
Wines usually come from one grape and one place
Aligoté and Gamay play smaller roles
Regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
Read Grand Cru and Premier Cru labels
Explain the size of each level

Burgundy's appellations form a pyramid. At the base, regional wines like Bourgogne, about half the production. Then village wines, named after a commune, like Gevrey-Chambertin. Then Premier Cru, named vineyards within a village, about 10%. At the top, 33 Grand Crus, about 1% of production.
Regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru

A village wine names the village. A Premier Cru adds the vineyard, like Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Clos Saint-Jacques. A Grand Cru names only the vineyard, like Chambertin or Montrachet. Many villages added their most famous Grand Cru to their name, so Gevrey became Gevrey-Chambertin. That can confuse: the village wine isn't the Grand Cru.
Grand Crus name only the vineyard
Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
Each level is smaller and more specific.

Because vineyards are split among many owners, a single climat can appear on many labels. Domaines grow and bottle their own grapes; négociants buy grapes or wine and bottle under their own name. Producer matters as much as appellation in Burgundy.
Producer matters as much as place
About how many Grand Crus does Burgundy have?
Burgundy's pyramid: regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
Grand Crus name only the vineyard
Domaines and négociants both bottle; producer matters
Describe the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune

The Côte d'Or runs about 50 km from Dijon to Santenay. The northern half, the Côte de Nuits, is almost all Pinot Noir and has most of the red Grand Crus. The southern half, the Côte de Beaune, makes both reds and the great white Grand Crus, like Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne.
Nuits for red; Beaune for both

The best vineyards lie mid-slope, at about 250 to 350 m. There, limestone and marl mix in thin, well-drained soils, the sun hits from the east, and cold air drains below. The slope's top is too thin and exposed; the bottom, richer and wetter, gives simpler wines. A road, the D974, roughly marks the border of good and lesser land.
Match each village to its main wine.
Each village has its own personality.

Vosne-Romanée is home to Romanée-Conti, one of the world's most expensive wines, a 1.8-hectare Grand Cru. Chambolle-Musigny is elegant; Nuits-Saint-Georges firm. In the Côte de Beaune, Pommard is sturdy, Volnay delicate, and Corton is the only red Grand Cru.
The Côte de Nuits is famous mainly for white wine.
Not true. It's almost all Pinot Noir; the great whites come from the Côte de Beaune.
The Côte de Nuits makes reds; the Côte de Beaune both
Mid-slope vineyards give the best wines
Each village, like Vosne or Meursault, has its own style
Describe the Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais

Chablis, isolated in the north, about 130 km from Dijon, is cooler than the Côte d'Or. Chardonnay grows on Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of tiny oyster fossils. Wines are lean, mineral and high in acidity. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and seven Grand Cru climats, like Les Clos and Valmur, on one south-west facing slope.

South of the Côte d'Or, the Côte Chalonnaise has villages like Mercurey and Givry for reds, and Rully and Montagny for whites, offering good value. The Mâconnais, further south and warmer, makes rounder Chardonnay: Mâcon-Villages, and Pouilly-Fuissé, which gained Premier Cru vineyards in 2020, and Saint-Véran.
What makes Chablis' Kimmeridgian soil distinctive?
It's full of tiny oyster fossils
Kimmeridgian marl contains countless fossilised oyster shells.

Chablis is lean and mineral, usually unoaked or lightly oaked. The Côte de Beaune is richer, with oak. The Mâconnais is rounder, fruitier and more affordable. All are Chardonnay, showing how much place and climate change it.
Which are Mâconnais or Chalonnaise wines?
Chablis is lean and mineral on Kimmeridgian soil
The Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais offer value
Reading Burgundy and eating with it

A Burgundy label shows the appellation, from Bourgogne to Grand Cru, the producer, the vintage, and whether it's a domaine or négociant. Mis en bouteille au domaine means estate-bottled. Monopole means a single owner holds the whole vineyard, like La Romanée-Conti. Vieilles vignes means old vines, but it isn't legally defined.

Because Burgundy is continental and risky, vintage matters a lot. Frost, hail and rain can halve a crop or dilute it. Warm vintages give riper, rounder wines; cool ones leaner, fresher wines. Good producers make good wine even in difficult years.
What does monopole mean on a Burgundy label?
A single owner holds the whole vineyard
A monopole belongs to one owner.

Red Burgundy suits roast chicken, duck, game birds, boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin, two dishes cooked with the region's wine. Époisses cheese suits both reds and whites. Chablis suits oysters and snails, escargots de Bourgogne; Meursault suits lobster and creamy chicken. Serve reds at 14 to 16 degrees.
Vieilles vignes is a legally defined term in Burgundy.
Not true. It means old vines, but there's no legal definition.
Labels show appellation, producer and vintage
Vintage matters greatly in continental Burgundy
Red Burgundy suits coq au vin; Chablis suits oysters
Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
Grand Cru is the top, about 1% of production.
Match each area to its wine.
Monks studied and enclosed the plots.
Burgundy usually blends many grapes in each wine.
Not true. Wines are usually one grape from one place.
Burgundy is continental, east-facing and limestone
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay express each climat
The pyramid runs from Bourgogne to 33 Grand Crus
Producer and vintage matter as much as place
